title: Read Outdoor Illuminance Tables Without Losing Their Meaning
description: Distinguish lux and footcandles, listed-point means, ratios and missing values using original fictional examples with clearly limited scope.
body:
Read Outdoor Illuminance Tables Without Losing Their Meaning

Published October 26, 2026 · Lumascapes website editorial

Begin with the quantity the table actually describes

An outdoor-lighting proposal can contain several numbers with different meanings. A product may list output in lumens, electrical power in watts and color temperature in Kelvin. A calculation sheet may instead show illuminance in lux at named points on a surface. These are not competing ways to rank the same thing. Reading the quantity and unit before reading the numeral helps you ask a specific question about the information supplied, rather than treating the largest number as the best design.

This guide concerns reading an illuminance table, not choosing illumination targets or conducting a field test. The original fictional rows below were written for arithmetic practice. They are not readings from a Pittsburgh property, predictions from lighting software, manufacturer specifications or Lumascapes project results. No meter was used, no fixture was tested and no design was approved. Keeping that distinction visible matters because a realistic-looking table can otherwise acquire an authority that its source does not support.

A useful first question is whether the table represents a calculation, a field measurement or an illustrative example. Next ask what surface, positions and operating condition it represents. A numerical summary is interpretable only within those definitions. If the accompanying document does not answer them, record the uncertainty and ask the author. Do not supply a missing method from your own assumptions. The reading skills here help prepare that conversation; they do not establish compliance, accessibility, electrical safety or suitability for a particular property.

Keep lux separate from lumens and appearance

NIST's SI unit table identifies lux, symbol lx, as the unit of illuminance and expresses it as lumens per square meter. In this limited reading context, think of illuminance as light incident on the stated surface. Lumens describe luminous flux, a different quantity. A product's lumen figure alone does not supply the illuminance at a particular place on a property. The document must connect the source, geometry and relevant calculation or measurement conditions before a point value has that meaning.

Do not divide a fixture's advertised output by the whole property area and label the answer a verified site reading. That shortcut assumes a distribution over a chosen area that the product number does not establish. The mathematical units may look plausible while the physical assumptions are absent. Likewise, do not convert Kelvin or watts into lux by relabeling a column. The separate color-output guide explains those product fields. This page focuses on the definitions and summaries of values already presented as illuminance.

Illuminance is also not a complete statement about perceived brightness, glare, appearance or a person's ability to navigate. A field observation and an illuminance value may both be useful without being interchangeable. Preserve the original question: perhaps someone is describing a bright source in their view, a surface that looks uneven or a concern at an entry. Do not replace that observation with a single table average and conclude that every aspect of the scene has been assessed or resolved.

Convert footcandles and lux without changing the underlying quantity

NIST's conversion table lists the footcandle-to-lux multiplier as 10.76391. For this teaching exercise, use that listed factor consistently. Multiplying one fictional footcandle by 10.76391 gives 10.76391 lux. Multiplying two gives 21.52782 lux. To reverse the direction, divide a lux value by 10.76391. The conversion changes the numerical scale and unit label; it does not change the modeled or measured illumination, create a new observation or validate the document's assumptions.

A sheet that shows two footcandles and another that shows approximately 21.53 lux may therefore be describing the same numerical magnitude after rounding. Do not call the second figure more than ten times brighter merely because its numeral is larger. Confirm that the locations and conditions also match before treating the rows as equivalents. Unit equivalence is necessary for a comparison of unlike labels, but it is not evidence that two documents cover the same surfaces, times or design versions.

Keep additional digits while calculating and round when presenting the final value. If a display uses two decimal places, label 21.53 lux as rounded rather than implying the original input was known to that precision. A conversion factor with many digits does not improve an instrument, a source estimate or a rounded input. Preserve the original value and unit alongside the converted column so another reader can trace the operation and distinguish reported precision from calculation precision.

Read the original six-point fictional schedule

The practice CSV contains six invented point identifiers, A through F, with two fictional scenarios. Scenario One has values of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 lux. Scenario Two has 7 lux at every point. Both have a six-point arithmetic mean of 7 lux because each column sums to 42 and contains six values. The identifiers are teaching labels only. They are not real locations, coordinates, fixture numbers or a measurement layout, and the scenarios are not proposed product options.

The same mean hides a different set of point values. Scenario One has a listed minimum of 2 and maximum of 12, while Scenario Two has a listed minimum and maximum of 7. The range, defined here as maximum minus minimum, is 10 lux in the first scenario and zero in the second. Those statements describe the six supplied entries. They do not establish what occurs between the points, outside them or under a different operating condition. An evenly valued example is not a recommendation for an evenly lit landscape.

The visible table and downloaded CSV deliberately include the full point lists instead of only an average. This lets you reproduce the sums and see what a summary omits. When a real proposal supplies only one aggregate number, ask for the information needed to understand its coverage. That request is different from demanding a particular target, grid or test protocol. This article does not prescribe a professional sampling method or determine which assessment is required for an actual project.

Define the ratio before interpreting its number

For Scenario One, the listed maximum divided by the listed minimum is 12 divided by 2, or 6. The arithmetic mean divided by the minimum is 7 divided by 2, or 3.5. The minimum divided by the mean is 2 divided by 7, approximately 0.2857. These are different ratios calculated from the same six entries. A heading such as uniformity without a formula can leave a reader uncertain which one is intended. Ask for the numerator, denominator and included points.

Scenario Two gives one for all three of those ratios because every entry is 7. That does not make the ratio a pass result. No project criterion, applicable standard, measurement coverage or purpose has been supplied in this exercise. A ratio can describe variation within a stated list while remaining insufficient to judge a design. Avoid copying a value from a report into a comparison without its formula; even the direction that looks numerically preferable can differ when a ratio is inverted.

If a denominator is zero, the corresponding division is undefined under ordinary arithmetic. If a required minimum is missing, a complete-list minimum-based ratio cannot be computed from the available list. Do not insert zero to force a calculation or substitute a favorable-looking denominator from another scenario. Record what is known, what is absent and which calculation remains unavailable. A clearly stated limitation is part of a useful result, rather than a blemish that should be removed to make a summary look finished.

Distinguish a listed-point average from an area average

Our six-point mean gives every supplied entry equal weight. That is a definition of this arithmetic exercise, not a claim that the six fictional points represent equal portions of a property. A group of closely clustered points can dominate an unweighted list if many entries come from one small region. The average of the entries is still correctly calculated, but describing it as the average across an entire yard would add a spatial interpretation that the point list does not establish.

A separate original example makes the difference visible. Suppose three invented equal-condition region summaries have values of 2, 8 and 14 lux. Their simple mean is 8. If, solely for a separate arithmetic illustration, they represent areas with weights 1, 1 and 4, the weighted calculation is the sum of 2 times 1, 8 times 1 and 14 times 4, divided by 6. That equals 11. The two averages answer different questions because the weights differ. No such areas or weights are asserted for the six-point CSV.

Before accepting an area description, ask how the report derives it. Are values point samples, cell summaries, a software output or another defined estimate? What boundary and exclusions apply? This guide supplies no method for turning arbitrary point readings into a reliable area estimate. Its weighted illustration shows why labels matter. It should not be copied as a survey design, used to choose sample locations or cited as evidence that an installation meets a lighting requirement.

Treat missing values as missing, not as darkness

A third fictional CSV column repeats Scenario One but leaves point C blank. The five known entries sum to 36, so their available-value mean is 36 divided by 5, or 7.2 lux. That describes only the five known entries. It is not the complete six-point mean. Entering zero for the blank would give 36 divided by 6, or 6, but that result depends on an invented zero. A missing observation and a recorded zero are different states and should remain distinguishable in a file.

If the missing value were later supplied as the authored Scenario One value of 6, the six-point mean would return to 7. This demonstrates the consequence of resolving one blank within the invented data; it is not an estimate of what an unknown field reading must be. The location of missing information also matters when calculating extrema. If the smallest entry is absent, the smallest known entry is not automatically the minimum of the full intended set.

A fourth fictional column omits A, whose base value was 2, and retains 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Its available-value mean is 8, and its known minimum is 4. Label both as available-value results. Calling 4 the complete-set minimum would hide the omission. When comparing scenarios, use matching coverage or explicitly describe the difference. Removing a low value and then claiming improvement from the higher summary would confuse a change in the list with a change in the underlying scene.

Check whether a unit change alters the summary

Multiplying every known lux value in a list by the same positive conversion factor preserves its ordering and its maximum-to-minimum ratio, provided the denominator is nonzero. For example, converting both 12 and 2 lux to footcandles divides both by 10.76391. Their ratio remains six. The converted average changes numerical scale, but a ratio of two values expressed consistently does not. A large change in such a ratio after conversion is a reason to check mixed units, rounding and coverage before interpreting the table.

A percent change also requires consistent units and the same denominator definition. An increase from a fictional point value of 2 to 4 lux is a doubling of that listed value, while the difference is 2 lux. It is not an increase of two percent. This is a separate arithmetic illustration, not a claim that doubling any point improves a scene or that fixture output can be doubled to produce that result. Retain both the amount difference and the comparison basis in any explanation.

Keep calculation conditions attached to the table

A real report may identify a calculation plane, height, orientation, product configuration or operating setting. Preserve those labels when copying the values. A horizontal surface and a vertical surface are not interchangeable merely because both use lux. Similarly, an initial calculation and one using a stated maintenance assumption may answer different questions. This article does not provide a universal adjustment factor, decay prediction or maintenance schedule. It teaches you to retain the assumptions actually stated rather than inventing one for a neat comparison.

If the document contains measured results, ask the responsible professional how the locations, conditions and instruments were documented. A meter model or calibration statement, where supplied, has its own scope; the presence of a number does not by itself validate a whole property assessment. If the document contains calculated results, ask which version of the input configuration it represents. Neither kind of result should be silently relabeled as the other. The fictional example is neither measured nor software-predicted and carries no calibration claim.

Document versions matter when a proposal changes. If fixture selection, layout or operating assumptions change, do not combine favorable values from different versions into an apparently single result. Keep a dated reference to the report and its revision. A summary may explain that two tables have different coverage or assumptions and therefore are not directly comparable. That is a useful conclusion. It is more accurate than forcing a ranking solely because each document offers an average and a minimum somewhere on the page.

Use photographs for context without inventing measurements

A photograph can help describe the location or viewpoint associated with a concern. It does not supply a trustworthy lux value simply because a surface looks light or dark in the image. Exposure, processing and display choices are part of the photographic context, so preserve an ordinary written description rather than reverse-engineering a numerical illuminance claim from a screenshot. The separate consultation-photo guide helps organize that handoff. Nothing here asks a homeowner to recreate a technical measurement procedure or alter a lighting system.

If an image is included beside a table, explain whether it is an illustrative concept, a site photograph or a diagram supplied by the report author. Do not assign the fictional A-through-F identifiers to real places without supporting documentation. Write a caption that states the image's purpose. If an editor needs help distinguishing captions from text alternatives, the related room-photo guide discusses that content question separately. That resource is not a photometric method, a statement about this installation or an accessibility certification.

A practical handoff can contain the original document, its version, the exact table heading, the unit, the stated location or surface, the question being asked and the unresolved information. Keep any personal identifying details limited to what the actual consultation requires. Ask the professional to explain the relevant report rather than requesting a change based only on our fictional figures. This guide makes no electrical operating instructions, installation steps, site-access directions or guarantees about visibility and navigation.

Write a summary that preserves both arithmetic and limits

A faithful summary of the original six-point cases says that both have a listed-point mean of 7 lux, while their listed minima and ranges differ. It states that the examples are invented and that no area coverage or suitability finding follows. A weak authored summary would say the equal averages prove identical lighting performance. That conclusion discards the differing point lists and adds a performance claim absent from the source. The weak sentence is written for teaching; it is not an observed AI output or a test of any product.

Review copied summaries for unit swaps, omitted blanks, changed denominators and claims about unrepresented areas. Recalculate a small example independently rather than checking only whether the prose sounds plausible. If a reported figure cannot be reproduced, identify the missing formula or source detail before alleging an error. An underlying method may use weights or coverage that your extract omitted. Preserve the source and question so the person responsible for the document can explain the calculation within its real scope.

The resulting conversation should be specific: which quantity, which unit, which points, which formula and which conditions? Those questions support a clearer understanding of a proposal without substituting a public teaching page for a property-specific assessment. Do not use these sample values as targets, evidence of adequate illumination, a way to approve work or a promise of comfort, safety, compliance or energy savings. They are a reproducible exercise in reading and describing a table honestly.

Frequently asked questions

Are lux and lumens interchangeable labels?

No. NIST distinguishes illuminance in lux from luminous flux in lumens. A fixture's output value does not establish illumination at a particular surface without the relevant context. Keep the field names and units intact. This guide does not calculate a property's illuminance from a fixture label or replace the separate product-color and output discussion.

How do I convert footcandles to lux in the example?

Multiply by the NIST-listed factor of 10.76391. Two fictional footcandles therefore correspond to 21.52782 lux using that factor, or approximately 21.53 when displayed to two decimal places. Reverse the direction by division. Conversion changes the unit representation, not the underlying observation, its precision, its coverage or the validity of its assumptions.

Do matching averages mean the point lists are the same?

No. Scenario One and Scenario Two both average 7 across six supplied points, but their minima, maxima and ranges differ. Review the point values and coverage alongside any aggregate. Neither the matching averages nor the differences establish a design preference or a property-performance result because this exercise supplies no actual installation, criteria or site assessment.

Can I enter zero for a blank value?

Not unless zero is actually the supported value under the source's definitions. Our missing-C column has five known values averaging 7.2. Inserting zero would produce a different calculation built on an invented observation. Label available-value summaries and preserve missing entries. Seek the absent information rather than treating an incomplete list as a completed measurement set.

Which uniformity ratio should I use to approve a proposal?

This guide supplies no approval criterion. Ask which formula and coverage the real document uses and how those relate to the appropriate project assessment. Maximum-to-minimum, mean-to-minimum and minimum-to-mean are distinct calculations. Their arithmetic examples do not establish a target, an applicable requirement, a measurement method or compliance with any standard.

Were these values measured by Lumascapes or generated by a model?

No. The values and summary contrasts were deliberately authored for this educational page. They are not property readings, lighting-software predictions, model observations, manufacturer test data or client outcomes. The page offers primary unit references and independently checked arithmetic, with no named professional review, certification, operating authorization or institutional endorsement.
